terms.gloss: a sign, a mark; of an illness, a symptom
evidence: Cels. 3.2: dēcēdentis ejus notae sunt, they are signs that it is abating
terms.comment: A mark or sign of any kind, which Celsus uses of the signs by which a doctor sees how an illness is going; Traupman gives it first for symptom. The illness goes in the genitive: notae morbī.

evidence: Cels. 3.2: acceduntque ea signa, quae priōre volūmine exposita sunt
terms.comment: Celsus uses signa and notae side by side; see sign.

evidence: M-O s.v. symptom: Caelius Aurelianus, Cassius Felix; in medical Latin since
terms.comment: Greek σύμπτωμα. Late Latin medical writers and modern medical Latin use it; Lewis & Short does not have it.

phrases.latin: ea vērō, quae contrāria hīs sunt, dēcēdentis ejus notae sunt
phrases.english: the opposite of these are signs that the illness is abating

sources: Lewis & Short: nota · Lewis & Short: signum · Lewis & Short: indicium
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 66, 388.
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. symptom.
